en: The Scripture on the Great Ānāpāna-smṛti Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
This scripture frequently uses the character "sui" (隨); except for the "sui" in "counting the breaths and following them" (*śvāsa-anuśvāsa*), all other instances are "duo" (墮) in other editions.
Translated during the Later Han dynasty by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, also known as the kingdom of Śāketa or the kingdom of Cānakya.

At that time, the Buddha sat in practice of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) for ninety days; he then sat alone for another ninety days, contemplating and calculating how to deliver and liberate the people of the ten directions, as well as all classes of beings, including those that fly and those that crawl.
Furthermore, as for my statement that I practiced *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) for ninety days: through *ānāpāna-smṛti*, one attains mastery over the mind of compassionate mindfulness;
having completed the practice of *ānāpāna-smṛti*, one further gathers the mind and practices mindfulness.
*Ānā* means the body; *apāna* means the breath; and guarding the mind is the Way.
Guarding is called restraint, which is also termed not transgressing the precepts;
restraint is also termed protection.
"Guarding" means universally protecting all things so that no transgression occurs.
"Intention" (yi) means the cessation of intention; it is also the Way.
"An" represents arising, and "pan" represents cessation. "Intention" serves as the causal condition, while "guarding" constitutes the Way.
"An" (śamatha) refers to counting; "pan" (vipaśyanā) refers to following along; "shouyi" (dhāraṇī/smṛti) refers to cessation.
"An" refers to mindfulness of the Way; "pan" refers to the unraveling of knots; "shouyi" refers to not falling into transgression.
"An" (peace) means avoiding transgression; "pan" (universal) means not entering into transgression; and "shouyi" (guarding the mind) is the Way. "An" is concentration;
"pan" is ensuring that nothing causes agitation; and "shouyi" is not allowing the mind to become disordered.
Anapanasmrti (安般守意) is called "governing the mind" to reach the attainment of the unconditioned (*asamskrta*).
"An" (安) signifies existence; "pan" (般) signifies non-existence.
If the mind contemplates existence, one cannot attain the Way.
If one conceives of non-existence, one does not attain the Way;
nor does one conceive of existence, nor does one conceive of non-existence—this accords with the concentration of emptiness, and the mind follows the practice of the Way.
"Existence" refers to the myriad things, while "non-existence" refers to doubt, which is also considered emptiness.
"An" (ā) is the fundamental causal condition; "pan" (prahāṇa) is the absence of a locus.
When a practitioner of the Way knows that the fundamental has nowhere from which it comes and also knows that cessation has no locus, this is called "guarding the mind."
"An" (āna) means purity; "pan" (apana) means clarity; "shou" (sthiti) means non-existence; and "yi" (samudaya) means arising. This is purity and the unconditioned (*asamskrta*).
"Non-existence" refers to living, and "being" refers to birth; because one no longer undergoes suffering, it is called living.
"An" (āna) refers to non-arising; "pan" (pra) refers to arising.
If the mind has not yet arisen, it is the guarding of the mind;
if the mind has already arisen, it is likewise the guarding of the mind.

If [the mind] has already arisen and the consciousness then wanders, it is because one does not maintain watchfulness; therefore, one must bring it back. For this reason, the Buddha taught *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).

"Āna" refers to the grasping of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and "apāna" refers to the abandoning of the five aggregates. "Smṛti" (mindfulness) refers to awakening to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) so as not to follow after body, speech, or mind.
Regarding "guarding the mind": to have no attachments is to guard the mind; to have attachments is not to guard the mind. Why is this?
Because the mind arises and then ceases.
When the mind no longer gives rise to [conceptual] thoughts for the sake of the Way, this is called guarding the mind (*manasikāra*).
Guarding the mind means not allowing the mind to arise; for arising leads to death, which is failing to guard the mind.
Do not allow the mind to die; for death leads to birth. When the mind neither dies nor arises, this is the Way.

The *Ānāpāna-smṛti* (Anban shouyi) possesses ten forms of wisdom (*jñāna*), namely: counting the breaths, following the breath, cessation, contemplation, returning to purity, and the Four Noble Truths. These constitute the accomplishment of the ten forms of wisdom; that is to say, the integration of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) constitutes the accomplishment of practice.
Maintaining mindfulness is like a lamp: it has two causes and conditions—
the first is to dispel darkness,
and the second is to perceive light.
Guarding the mind:
first, destroying delusion;
second, perceiving wisdom.
Guarding the mind: since the mind arises from causes and conditions, one should attend to those causes and conditions without attachment; this is what is meant by guarding the mind.
There are three grades of guarding the mind:
first, guarding it so that [defilements] do not arise.
Second, that which has already arisen should be swiftly extinguished;
third, regarding actions already performed, one should feel regret and resolve not to commit them again for billions of kalpas.

Guarding (*śīla*) and intention (*citta*) are each distinct: guarding all objects of perception throughout the ten directions so as not to transgress is "guarding"; awakening to that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is "intention"—this is the practice of guarding the mind.
Within the guarding of the mind, there are four kinds of joy:
first, the joy of knowing the essentials;
second, the joy of knowing the Dharma.
Third, for the sake of knowing the joy of cessation;
fourth, for the sake of knowing what is truly joyful.
These are the four joys.
Taking the Dharma as practice and attainment as the Way, the six matters of guarding the mind have both external and internal aspects:
counting, following, and stopping are external; contemplation, returning, and purification are internal.
This is to follow the Path. Why is this so?

Because mindfulness and the breaths follow one another, and through cessation and contemplation, they return to purity; for when the mind's habitual tendencies incline toward the Path, it follows the Path.
If one departs from these six matters, one instead follows the world.

Counting the breath is for restraining the mind; following the sign is for collecting the mind; cessation is for stabilizing the mind; contemplation is for detaching the mind; returning is for unifying the mind; and purification is for guarding the mind.
Because one cannot control the mind through the use of persons, one practices these six matters.
For what reason does one count the breaths?
Because the mind is distracted.
Why is it that they do not attain it?
Because they lack recognition.
Why is it that they do not attain dhyāna?
This is because one practices without abandoning, exhausts the habitual tendencies, realizes the fruit, and cultivates the path.

Counting the breath is the ground; following the breath is the plow; cessation is the yoke; contemplation is the seed; returning is the rain; and purification is the cultivation. Through these six matters, one follows the Path.

Counting the breath cuts off the external; following the sign cuts off the internal. Stopping is for the cessation of transgressions; practicing contemplation is for the withdrawal of the mind. Not receiving worldly things is "returning"; the severance of mindfulness is "purity."

When the mind is distracted, one should count the breaths; when the mind is settled, one should follow the signs; when the mind seeks to sever [defilements], one should practice cessation; when the mind has attained the Way, one should contemplate; when not turning toward the five aggregates, one should return; and when there is nothing whatsoever, it shall be pure.

When there are many affairs, one should practice counting the breaths; when there are few affairs, one should follow the signs. When the mind within the household is exhausted, one should practice cessation. Fearing the world, one should practice contemplation; not desiring the world, one turns back; the severance of thoughts constitutes purity.
For what reason does one count the breaths?
It is because one does not wish to follow after the five aggregates.
For what reason does one follow after the signs?
It is because one wishes to know the five aggregates.
Why does one practice cessation?
It is because one wishes to contemplate the five aggregates.
For what reason does one contemplate the aggregates?
Because one wishes to know the fundamental nature of the body.
For what reason does one know the fundamental nature of the body?
It is for the sake of abandoning suffering.
Why does one return? It is because of weariness with birth and death.
For what reason is it purified?
Because one does not grasp at the five aggregates through discernment.
Thus, by following the eightfold path of wisdom, one attains the fulfillment of one's aspirations.

When practicing the breath, one follows the counting; when following the signs, one follows mindfulness; when abiding, one follows concentration; when observing, one follows purification; when returning, one follows intention; and when purifying, one follows the Path, which is also called following practice.

Counting the breath constitutes the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); following along constitutes the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); cessation constitutes the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); contemplation constitutes the five faculties (*indriya*) and the five powers (*bala*); returning constitutes the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); and purification constitutes the eightfold path (*mārga*).
To attain stillness without following [the breath] is not "guarding the mind";
to attain following without stopping is not "guarding the mind";
to attain stopping without observing is not "guarding the mind."
To attain the contemplation of non-returning is not yet the guarding of the mind;
to attain the returning of impurity is not yet the guarding of the mind;
only when one attains purity and further purifies it does one truly guard the mind.

Having already practiced mindfulness of breathing, evil does not arise; yet one counts again in order to collectively restrain the mind so that it does not follow after the six sense-decadences (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Practicing with following is for the sake of wishing to leave the six sense-decadences; practicing with stopping is for the sake of wishing to repel the six sense-decadences; practicing with observing is for the sake of wishing to sever the six sense-decadences; practicing with returning is for the sake of wishing not to receive the six sense-decadences; practicing with purification is for the sake of wishing to extinguish the six sense-decadences.
Once [the breath] has been extinguished, one then follows the Path.
Counting the breaths is intended to restrain the mind; since there are long and short intervals within the breath, one must further restrain this mind that perceives length and brevity.
For what reason does one guard the mind?
It is because one wishes to cease evil.
Evil can be guarded against, yet it cannot be guarded against.
Why is this? Because evil has already been exhausted, it need not be guarded against further.
There are three matters regarding the counting of breaths:
First, one should practice while seated;
second, upon seeing forms, one should contemplate their impermanence and impurity;
third, one should clearly understand anger, resentment, doubt, jealousy, and the recollection of the past.
Regarding distraction during counting the breaths: one should recognize the conditions from which it arises and understand that this pertains to the internal mind.
Distraction during the first breath is a fault of the external mind, because the breath enters from without;
distraction during the second breath is a fault of the internal mind, because the breath issues from within.
The third, fifth, seventh, and ninth belong to the external mind; the fourth, sixth, eighth, and tenth belong to the internal mind.
Envy, ill will, and doubt—these three mental states belong to the internal;
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech—these seven mental states and other such matters belong to the external.
When the breath is perceived, it is considered external; when the breath is not perceived, it is considered internal.

The breath arises from the mind; when mindfulness and the breath are unified as one, one counts the breath until the count is exhausted. Whether it is counted as one or not one depends on whether the mind is directed outward, for the breath has not yet ceased.
It is like counting money: if one’s intention is on the number five, yet one counts it as one.

As for why one first counts the inhalation when counting the breaths—it is because there are seven evils externally and three evils internally; since the few cannot overcome the many, one therefore first counts the inhalation.
Those who fail to master counting the breaths do so because they have lost the original intent.
The original intent refers to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Because they lose this intent and fall into perversion, they also lose their teacher.
Regarding the teacher: when first sitting, one should practice in sequence once the first inhalation brings peace to the body;
if one loses this original intent, one will not attain stillness.

In counting the breaths, the mind should constantly contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; one should calculate that the exhaled breath ceases and the inhaled breath likewise ceases.
Once this is known, one has attained the Way; one must swiftly maintain a mind of dread regarding impermanence.
When one attains this state of mind, one immediately attains cessation.
As for why the inhalation and exhalation differ: exhalation constitutes the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), while inhalation constitutes the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha);
at other times, exhalation constitutes the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), while inhalation constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
Using these as distinctions, a practitioner of the Path should discern these three intentions:
inhalation is for not receiving offenses; exhalation is for eliminating offenses; and guarding the mind is for departing from offenses.
Inhalation is the condition for receiving; exhalation is the condition for reaching; guarding the mind is the condition for non-separation.
If one fails to achieve counting the breaths, there are three causes and conditions:
first, the arrival of transgressions.
Second, the practice is inconsistent;
third, there is a lack of diligence.
When the inhalation is short and the exhalation is long, having no mental focus constitutes the intent for the Way, whereas having a specific object of thought constitutes a transgression.
Evil lies outside, not within.

When counting the breaths, there is a distracted mind regarding the inhalation as long and the exhalation as short; when the practice of breathing is unsettled, it is considered long, and when it is concentrated, it is considered short.
To be mindful of the myriad things is the long breath; to have nothing to be mindful of is the short breath.
If one has not yet reached ten breaths and the count is broken, one begins anew; reaching ten breaths constitutes a short breath.
The inhalation is perceived as short; why is this?
Because one ceases and no longer counts it.
The exhalation is also perceived as long; why is this?
Because the breath does not cease, it is called "long.
One knows the long exhalation for oneself, and one knows the short exhalation for oneself:

this means that wherever the mind is directed constitutes knowing the length for oneself; when the mind perceives the length, it is "knowing for oneself," and when the mind does not perceive the length, it is "not knowing for oneself."
When a practitioner of the Way practices *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) desiring to still the mind, by what causes and conditions can they achieve this stilling?
Listen as I explain *ānāpāna-smṛti*: what is meant by "āna" (in-breath)?
What is ānāpāna? *Āna* is defined as inhalation;
*apāna* is defined as exhalation. To maintain mindfulness of the breath without distraction is called *ānāpāna*.
As for "guarding the mind," it means desiring to bring the mind to stillness.

For the practitioner and the beginner, there are four types of practice for the mindfulness of ānāpāna (breath-counting), which eliminate the two evils and the sixteen stages of mastery; one immediately knows this for oneself as the practice of mindfulness of ānāpāna, thereby bringing the mind to stillness.
What are the four kinds?
First is counting, second is following, third is settling, and fourth is observing.
What are the two evils?
Do not let [the breath] exceed ten counts, nor let it fall short of ten.
What are the sixteen stages of mastery?
At that very moment, one knows for oneself whether the breathing is long;
One immediately knows for oneself that the breath is short;
one immediately knows for oneself that the breath moves the body;
one immediately knows for oneself that the breath is subtle.
He knows for himself that his breathing is easy;
he knows for himself that his breathing is difficult;
he knows for himself that his breathing has ceased.
He immediately knows for himself when his breathing is unceasing;
he immediately knows for himself when his breathing is accompanied by a joyful mind;
he immediately knows for himself when his breathing is not accompanied by a joyful mind.
He immediately knows within himself that his thoughts of the myriad things have already passed and can no longer be recovered; he knows this through his own breath.
Within, there is nothing further to contemplate; he knows this through his own breath.
Having cast off all that was contemplated, he knows this through his own breath.
He knows his own breathing when he does not abandon what he contemplates;
he knows his own breathing when he relinquishes his body and life;
he knows his own breathing when he does not relinquish his body and life.
These are the sixteen ways of self-knowledge at that very moment.
Question:
What is meant by "neither exceeding ten nor falling short of ten"?
Response:
To count when the breath has already ceased is an excess; to count before the breath has ceased is a deficiency.
To lose the count is also faulty, and to fall short of the count is also faulty; these constitute the two faults.
When the second breath becomes disturbed, it is called a short breath; when the ninth breath becomes disturbed, it is called a long breath; attaining the tenth breath is called a comfortable breath.
When they follow one another, it is subtle. If the mind is set upon the long breath, one then shifts the mind, thinking:
"For what reason do I contemplate the long?"
When the mind is directed toward brevity, one immediately realizes that one must not allow the mind to dwell; for dwelling constitutes attachment.
To "abandon body and life" refers to the practice of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing).
Having attained the intention of the Path, one then abandons body and life.
Because one has not yet attained the aspiration for the Way and constantly cherishes the body, one does not relinquish life or limb.

Subtle and minute respiration constitutes the Way, while long [respiration] constitutes birth and death; short respiration is movement that constitutes birth and death, whereas [long respiration] is short in relation to the Way. Why is this so?
Because one has not attained the mind of the Way and lacks knowledge and vision, it is considered deficient.

Counting the breaths is the single; following them is the double; cessation is the single-mindedness; contemplation is the knowing of the mind; returning is the practicing of the Way; and purification is the entering of the Way.
Counting the breaths constitutes *smṛti* (mindfulness); reaching ten breaths constitutes *dhāraṇā* (retention). This is external dhyāna.
Mindfulness of the impurity of the body in accordance with emptiness is internal dhyāna.
When the methods of dhyāna do not accept what is evil as it comes, this is called "rejection."
Close the mouth and count the breaths, following the air as it enters and exits, knowing where the air originates and where it ceases.
If the mind has thoughts, one must not count the breaths;
if there is slowness or rapidity, or if the breaths are large or small, one likewise must not count them.
When the ears hear sounds and become distracted, one likewise cannot maintain the count.

When counting the breaths, the mind must be fixed on the breath; if the counting is unskillful, the practice fails. Only when the application of the mind is focused upon the mind itself does one attain *śamatha*.
If one counts the breaths while the mind remains fixed solely on the breath, this is not skillful.
One should know where the mind arises and where the breath ceases; when one thus accords with the counting and the conditions are exhausted, one will attain concentration of mind.
To guard the mind means to be mindful of the inhalation and exhalation of breath. Once one is mindful of the breath, evil thoughts do not arise; therefore, it is called guarding the mind.
One perceives that the breath arises through causes and conditions and ceases when there are no causes and conditions;
when causes and conditions are severed, the breath comes to rest.
Counting the breath is ultimate sincerity; the breath not being disturbed is patience.
As the breath becomes subtle through counting, one no longer perceives its inhalation or exhalation; in this way, one should maintain the cessation of a single thought.
Breathing exists both within the body and without; it arises due to causes and conditions, and because karmic offenses have not yet been exhausted, there is breathing.
When causes and conditions are severed, breathing no longer arises.
Counting the breath is considered the preliminary stage of the second dhyāna. Why is this?
Because it does not depend on mental application (*vitarka*), it is the preliminary stage of the second dhyāna.
Counting the breaths is not guarding the mind; mindfulness of the breath is what constitutes guarding the mind.
When the breath enters from without and has not yet ceased, the attention is on the entry; when it has reached its end, the consciousness is on the counting.

The ten breaths have ten mental states which constitute ten fetters; the two states that follow one another constitute two fetters; and the state of cessation constitutes one mental state which is one fetter.
If one cannot count the breaths, it is due to an unwholesome mind and cannot be bound;
only when the unwholesome mind ceases can one count, which is called the harmonious and agreeable fetter.

Having attained the abandoning of inhalation, one abandons inhalation; having attained the abandoning of exhalation, one abandons exhalation; having attained the abandoning of following along, one abandons following along; having attained the abandoning of stilling, one abandons stilling; having attained the abandoning of contemplation, one abandons contemplation, and does not return to them.
To not return means not to count them again.
The breath also governs the mind, and the mind also governs the breath;
when there is something being thought of, the breath governs the mind, and when there is nothing being thought of, the mind governs the breath.
There are four matters regarding the breath:
The first is wind, the second is qi, the third is breath, and the fourth is panting.
That which has sound is wind; that which is without sound is qi; the coming and going [of breath] is respiration; and when the coming and going of qi is incomplete, it is panting.

Counting the breath cuts off the external; following the breath cuts off the internal. Counting as the breath enters from the outside is for cutting off the external; this is also intended to leave behind external conditions. Counting as the breath goes out from within is intended to leave behind internal conditions.
Physical seclusion is external, while mental seclusion is internal;
physical and mental seclusion are what constitute following along, whereas the inhalation and exhalation of breath are the two matters.
Counting the breath is intended to sever internal and external conditions.
What are the internal and external?
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the internal; form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects are the external.
Practicing the mindfulness of breathing is intended to direct the mind toward emptiness, merely desiring to cease other mental activities.
Why is it directed toward emptiness?
Because within the breath there is nothing to be done.
When counting the breaths, does the mind wander?
If one immediately becomes aware of this, it is because the transgression is heavy while the mind is light; the transgression draws the mind away so swiftly that one does not notice it.

Once the practice of the Way has resulted in attaining the breath, one naturally grows weary of the breath and the intention to count it; wishing to turn away from it and no longer desiring to count—this is what constitutes attaining the breath.
The same applies to the cessation of the signs associated with śamatha and vipaśyanā.
To know that the inhalation and exhalation have ceased is the sign of attaining cessation;
to know that birth and death are no longer operative is the sign of attaining the cessation of birth and death.
Having attained the fourth dhyāna, one should simply contemplate emptiness as the seed for cultivating the Way.

Once concentration has been attained through the practice of breath-regulation (ānāpāna), and one no longer perceives the inhalation and exhalation of the vital energy (prāṇa), one may then proceed with contemplation.
First, one should contemplate fifty-five matters;
second, one should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination within the body.
Question:
"In the inhalation and exhalation of breath, is there a fixed location?
He replied:
"When the breath enters, that is its location; when the breath exits, that is its location."
Counting the breath while sitting, such that pain-itching, perception, volition, and consciousness cease and do not function—this is what it means to sit.
One attains the Way by recollecting the breath; as for further analytical calculation, it is because the breath itself is devoid of cognition.
Question:
If one attains the Way through mindfulness of breathing, why is it said that there is nothing to be known? Answer:
The mind knows the breath, but the breath does not know the mind; this is what is meant by "having nothing known.
When a person is unable to examine the mind through calculation, they are made to count the breaths in order to bring the mind to stillness.
Although one practices counting the breaths, evil does not arise.
Lacking wise insight, by what practice can one attain such wisdom?
From one to ten, one discerns concentration and distraction, and recognizes the application of remedies for each state.
Having attained concentration of mind, one then follows with wisdom; the attainment of analytical calculation constitutes the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Question: What is counting?
Answer: "Number" refers to the objective entity (*vastu*).
For example, when a person has one matter and seeks another, this constitutes a "numbered offense."
When calculating the merit of a practitioner of the Way, why is it fixed at ten?
A single thought arising constitutes one; two thoughts arising constitute two. The count culminates at ten, reaching ten to complete the total; therefore, it is said that ten counts constitute merit.
Furthermore, there is another kind of transgression: it is a transgression because one is unable to extinguish the breath;
it is also said to be a transgression when the cycle of birth and death of the mind does not cease, such that after falling into the world, one fails to sever the affairs of the mundane world.

The six sense-faculties constitute six matters; together with sensation, perception, volition, birth-and-death, and consciousness, these form ten matters, which correspond to the ten internal breaths.

Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, frivolous speech, envy, anger, and delusion correspond to the ten external breaths, meaning they are to be ceased and not practiced.
Question:
What are the sixteen matters? Answer:

The "ten matters" refers to counting; up to the "sixteen matters" refers to counting, following the characteristics, cessation, contemplation, returning, and purification. These constitute the sixteen matters, which serve as the practice that is never abandoned and follow the Path.
Question:
When counting the breaths, one contemplates the wind as following form; how does this accord with the Path? Answer:
The practice of the mind consists in not dwelling on form, so that when the breath ceases, it is extinguished; one falls into impermanence, and knowing impermanence is the Way.
A practitioner who wishes to attain the Way must understand the two matters of sitting and walking:
the first is sitting, and the second is walking.
Question:
Are sitting and walking the same or different? Answer:
Sometimes they are the same, and sometimes they are different.
Counting the breath, following, stopping, contemplating, returning, and purifying—these six matters are sometimes for sitting and sometimes for walking.
Why is this? Counting the breath while the mind is settled is "sitting"; the mind following the Dharma is "walking.
When the mind has already arisen and does not depart, that is both "walking" and "sitting."
Regarding the method of sitting meditation: one does not count two as one, nor does one count one as two.
To "count two as one" means that before the first breath is finished, one says "two"; this is counting two as one, which constitutes excessive diligence.
To "count one as two" means that once the breath has already entered the second [count], one only then says "one"; this is counting one as two, which constitutes insufficient diligence.
From three to four, five to six, seven to eight, and nine to ten, each has its own division and should be distinguished according to its category;
counting one as one and two as two constitutes the practice of the Dharma, whereby one falls into diligent application.
There are three ways of sitting that lead to the Path:
first, sitting while counting the breaths; second, sitting while reciting the sutras; third, sitting with joy upon hearing the sutras—these are the three.
There are three grades of sitting:
first, sitting associated with attachment to flavor; second, pure sitting; and third, sitting free from fetters.
What is sitting associated with attachment to flavor?
This means that when the mind remains attached to its activity without departing from it, this is called sitting in union with flavor (*āsvādanasamprayukta*).
What is meant by sitting in purity (*śuddha*)?
It means not being mindful [of such attachment] is sitting in purity.
What is the sitting without fetters?
It is the sitting without fetters because all fetters have been exhausted.
There are three grades of cessation:
First is mixed breathing, second is pure breathing, and third is the breath of the Path.
Not practicing the Path constitutes mixed breathing;
counting up to ten breaths without distraction constitutes pure breathing.
Having attained the Way, this constitutes the cessation of the Way.
There are three grades of cessation:
there is great cessation, middling cessation, and subtle cessation.
When there is speech from the mouth, the coarse breath ceases;
when one contemplates the Path, the intermediate breath ceases;
and upon attaining the fourth dhyāna, the subtle breath ceases.
Question:
Why did the Buddha teach people to practice counting the breaths and guarding the mind? Answer:
There are four causes and conditions:
first, because one does not desire suffering;
second, because one seeks to avoid a distracted mind.
Third, because of the condition of being obstructed, one does not wish to encounter birth and death;
fourth, because of the desire to attain the path of Nirvana.
To provide an analogy for why the sun might be said to lack radiance, there are four causes and conditions:
First, because of the presence of clouds;
second, because of the presence of dust;
third, because of the presence of great winds.
Fourth, because there is smoke.
There are also four causes and conditions for being unable to count the breaths:
first, because one employs mindfulness of birth and death and engages in discursive calculation.
Second, because of consuming too much food and drink;
third, because of extreme exhaustion;
fourth, because while sitting one cannot further attain the ground of purification.
When these four conditions arise, each has its characteristic sign:
while sitting and counting the breaths, if one suddenly thinks of other matters and loses the mindfulness of the breath, this is the sign of discursive calculation;
if all the joints ache and one cannot sit for long, this is the sign of overeating.
The body feels heavy and the mind is dazed, desiring only to sleep; this is the sign of extreme exhaustion.
Sitting on all four sides, unable to take even a single breath; this is the sign of the ground of transgression.
Knowing one's transgressions, one should practice walking meditation;
if one reads the scriptures while seated and does not allow the mind to habituate to sin, misfortune will likewise be extinguished.
Those who practice the Way should always keep the fundamental in mind.
What is the root? It is mind, thought, and consciousness that constitute the root.
These three things are all unobservable; having arisen, they immediately perish. When the fundamental mind no longer arises, one attains this mind as the mind of the Path.
When the original intention has already ceased, there is no further conditioning for the arising of suffering; it is simply cut off.
As the concentrated mind becomes increasingly superior day by day, this is what constitutes concentration.

At times one attains concentration through the breath, at times through following signs, at times through cessation, and at times through contemplation; one proceeds directly according to whichever conditions for attaining concentration are encountered.
The practice of breath control also falls into greed. Why is this?
Because the mind becomes joyful when it is concentrated.
One should then calculate that as the exhalation and inhalation cease, the breath arises and the body arises.
The breath ceases and the body ceases;
yet one has not yet escaped the suffering of birth and death. Why is this?
Because one has already conceptualized joy, and thus craving arises even as it subsides.
When counting the breaths, one desires them to be rapid; when following the breaths, one desires them to be slow.
At times, when counting the breaths, they should be calm and gradual; at times, when following the breaths, they should be rapid. Why is this?
When counting the breaths, if the mind is not distracted, one should be calm and slow; if the counting becomes confused, one should count more rapidly. It is the same when following the breath.

In the first stage, both counting and following occur; although the objects of attention differ, even while counting the breaths, one must know the inhalation and exhalation of the air, yet the mind remains fixed upon the counting itself.
Counting the breaths, one further practices "following.
Regarding "stopping and observing" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), this refers to not grasping at the breath;
it is the stopping and observing that follows [the breath] based on habitual tendencies from previous lives.
Although one may attain this accompaniment, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must still arise from counting the breaths.

When the mind does not depart from the counting of breaths, this is called "the dharma being separated [from defilement]"; it is not the case that the counting of breaths is non-dharmic. If the mind does not follow after transgressions, yet the mind remains within the world, one then falls into transgression.

Counting the breath is for the purpose of not allowing the mind to become distracted. When the mind, being undistracted, proceeds in accordance with its object, one realizes that the preceding stage of the mind is known as *śamatha* (calm abiding).
*Śamatha* is identical to *vipaśyanā* (insight), and both are identical to *viśuddhi* (purity).
Regarding "when practicing the path and attaining a subtle state of mind, one should reverse the mind," this means one should again practice counting the breaths.
If, after reciting the scriptures, one again practices the subtle state of mind in meditation, this refers to not counting the breaths and instead practicing the method of following the breath.

The Buddha possesses six purities of intention, namely: counting the breath, following the breath, cessation, contemplation, returning, and purification; these six matters are able to restrain that which has no form.
The breath is both the mind and not the mind. Why is this?
At the time of counting, the mind abides in the breath; thus it is the mind.
Before long, the mind and the breath each proceed on their own; this is what is meant by "non-mind.
Once the breath has arisen from the mind, it ceases and there is no longer any mind.
It is not that people employ the mind, but rather that the mind employs people.
To "cause the mind" refers to counting the breaths, following the breath, cessation, contemplation, returning, and purification.
To recite the *Saptatriṃśat-dharmasūtra* (the Sutra on the Thirty-seven Factors) is what is meant by causing the mind;
when a person does not practice the Way but greedily pursues their desires, this is what is meant by the mind causing the person.
The breath has impurities; as long as these impurities of the breath are not removed, one cannot attain stillness.
What constitutes the impurities of the breath?
They are said to be the most violent among the three darknesses; this is what constitutes the impurities of the breath.
What are the three obscurations?
They refer to when the three poisons arise, there is an internal obscuration within the body; therefore, they are called the three obscurations.
The three poisons are:
First is greed and lust, second is anger and hatred, and third is ignorance and delusion.
People all die because of these three things; therefore, they are called poisons.
When counting the breaths, the mind should be focused on counting the breaths.
Within a short time, there are three kinds of mental states:
wholesome thoughts, unwholesome thoughts, and thoughts that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome.

One who wishes to know whether a person has attained the sign of cessation (*nirodha-nimitta*) should observe all phenomena and various beautiful forms; if the mind no longer clings to them, this is the attainment of cessation.
If the mind remains attached to signs, this is called "not yet attained," and one must exert even greater diligence.
Regarding the practice of exhausting the household mind: the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the household mind, and craving for all things constitutes the household mind.
"To follow along" means that by practicing wholesome dharmas, one attains liberation; thus, one should follow along with them.
It also means not following the five aggregates or the six sense bases, but rather following along with the breath and the mind.
Question:
For what reason is the third *śamatha* focused on the tip of the nose? Answer:

By means of counting, following, stopping, contemplating, returning, and purifying, all [breaths] enter and exit through the nose; because the mind habituates itself to this familiar location, it is also easy to recognize. For this reason, one fixes [the attention] on the tip of the nose.
When evil intentions arise, sever them through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); at times they cease at the tip of the nose, and at times they cease within the heart;
wherever they attach is where they cease.
When depravity comes to disturb the mind, simply observe one thing directly. When various evils come, the mind must not be moved; this is because the mind is fearless.

There are four kinds of cessation (*śamatha*): first, cessation through counting; second, cessation through following the signs; third, cessation through the tip of the nose; and fourth, cessation through calming the mind.
As for "cessation," it refers to the five pleasures and the six sense bases, which one must restrain and bring to a halt.
When the inhalation reaches its limit, it stops at the tip of the nose; this means that evil no longer enters and thus stops at the tip of the nose.

When the exhalation reaches its limit, it remains fixed at the tip of the nose; this means that the mind no longer departs from the body to move toward evil, and thus remains fixed at the tip of the nose.

It is also said that when the breath first enters, one directs the single thought toward non-arising and does not turn back; even the inhalation and exhalation are no longer perceived—this is "cessation" (śamatha).

As for "stopping" (śamatha): when exhaling and inhaling in accordance with suchness, one is aware of the preceding mental state as it emerges, but is not aware of the subsequent mental state as it emerges.

Being aware of the preceding mental state, one contemplates its characteristics; then, observing the inhalation and exhalation, one perceives their decay. One then experiences a dread of the characteristics of birth and death, withdraws the mind, and follows the characteristics of the mind directed toward the Path.

Do not follow after external signs; simply focus your mindfulness on the tip of the nose. Do not further contemplate the causal conditions of the five aggregates. When transgressions are severed and the mind is extinguished, one ceases even to breathe—this is cessation.

"Do not follow after signs" means that one should no longer direct the mind toward the inhalation and exhalation following the conditions of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), nor should one continue to breathe [with such attachment].

Regarding the fourth contemplation: it is the contemplation of the time when the breath fails; it is distinct from the contemplation of the body. One perceives that there is arising through causes and conditions, and cessation without causes and conditions.

Regarding the characteristic of mental reception (*manasaṃvedanālakṣaṇa*): it refers to when the mind desires to obtain something, yet the intellect calculates that the conditions for its attainment will inevitably perish; thereupon, one severs the desire and no longer pursues it—this is the characteristic of mental reception.

Regarding "contemplating together with consciousness as its causal condition": this means that consciousness cognizes the causal conditions of the five aggregates; one contemplates the out-breath and likewise contemplates the in-breath.
To "contemplate" refers to contemplating the five aggregates; this constitutes "contemplation together."
One should also observe the mind with the mind through two causal conditions: to sever evil within and to maintain mindfulness of the Path.

Regarding the observation that exhalation is distinct from inhalation: this means that exhalation constitutes the aggregate of birth-and-death (*saṃskāra-skandha*), while inhalation constitutes the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*);
at other times, exhalation constitutes the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), and inhalation constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Arising according to causes and conditions, the aggregates (skandhas) are immediately received; where the mind is directed, there is no constancy. For this reason, they are distinct; a practitioner of the Path should discern and know this.
This is also called: when the out-breath ceases, the in-breath arises;
when the in-breath ceases, the out-breath arises.
"Because of non-existence" means that regarding the human mind and all things, the mind arises and then ceases, and things are born and then die; this is what is meant by "because of non-existence.
Exhalation is not inhalation, and inhalation is not exhalation.

It does not mean that when exhaling the mind does not attend to inhalation, or when inhaling the mind does not attend to exhalation; rather, they are called "not [the same]" because the objects of attention are different.
"Middle faith" refers to entering the path, perceiving the causes and conditions of the path, and believing in the path; this constitutes middle faith.
The fifth, "further discarding the fetters," refers to discarding the seven evils of the body.
The sixth, "purifying the discarding of fetters," refers to discarding the three evils of the mind; this is termed "returning."
"Returning" means that the mind no longer gives rise to evil;
"evil" refers to non-returning. "Returning the body" means returning to evil.
Upon attaining the fifth stage of return, one both possesses a body and does not possess a body.
Why is this? When there is intention there is a body; when there is no intention there is no body. Intention is the seed of humanity; this is what is called "return."
"Returning" means that the mind does not again give rise to evil;
"not returning" refers to the arising of evil. Furthermore, it is said that the former [actions] assist the body and the latter assist the mind.
Not killing, stealing, committing sexual misconduct, engaging in double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, or frivolous chatter—these are what assist the body.
Freedom from envy, anger, and delusion constitutes the aid to the mind.
As for "returning the five aggregates": it is like purchasing gold and receiving stones instead; one then casts them aside on the ground and makes no further use of them.
All people greedily crave the five aggregates, yet upon encountering suffering, they no longer desire them—this is what is meant by returning the five aggregates.
What is meant by "directly seeing the place of cessation"? It refers to non-existence as being the place of cessation.
Question:
Since there is already nothing existing, for what reason is it called a "place"?
The sphere of nothingness has four abodes:
first, birds take the air as their abode;
second, arhats take nirvana as their abode.
Third, the Path takes non-existence as its locus;
fourth, the Dharma resides in the locus of contemplation.

To experience the characteristics of the five aggregates through the out-breath and in-breath refers to the mind’s wrong thoughts; by swiftly turning back toward correctness to give rise to awakening and sever [delusion], one experiences the characteristics of the five aggregates.
Regarding "reception" (vedanā), it refers to the characteristic of receiving and not receiving.
By perceiving the characteristics of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), one knows where [suffering] arises and where it ceases.

As for cessation, it refers to the reception of the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda); a person is born from the twelve links of dependent origination, and likewise dies from the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Not dwelling on thoughts" means not dwelling on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

To know where they arise and where they cease is to understand that the causal conditions of good and evil give rise to them and then cause them to perish; this is what is called the body, and it is also called the arising and ceasing of vital energy (*prāṇa*).
If one thinks, one lives; if one does not think, one dies. The mind and the body are identical; this is the severing of the path of birth and death.
Within this cycle of birth and death, all evil matters arise from the mind.

That "the present does not become the past, and the past does not become the present" means that what was previously contemplated has already ceased, and the present thought is not the previous thought;
it also means that the deeds performed in a previous life and the deeds performed in the present life each receive their own respective merit;
and it also means that the good one practices now is not the same as the evil one practiced previously.
It is also said that the present breath is not the previous breath, and the previous breath is not the present breath.
For those who engage in the discrimination of birth and death, they hold that when thought arises, there is birth; when thought ceases, there is cessation.
Therefore, regarding birth and death, one should distinguish between the myriad things and the body.
The merit of the past and future will eventually be exhausted. Why is this so?
All that arises perishes immediately, and what perishes is exhausted;
having known this exhaustion, one should strive with all one's might to bring it to an end.
To perceive that from above there is nowhere from which anything comes is to realize that for humans there is nowhere from which they come; it is the arising of the mind that constitutes the person.
Furthermore, it is said that if a person does not create [their own rebirth] when they come, there must be a place from which they come;
whereas if a person creates it themselves and experiences it themselves, there is no place from which they come.

Regarding what should be distinguished concerning birth and death: it means knowing how to distinguish the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and it also means knowing how to distinguish the birth and death of the mind.
If one conceives of the human mind as permanent, yet knows that it is not permanent, this too is a form of discrimination.

As for "later seeing no place [for it]," this means that although one does not currently see the sinner within the cycle of birth and death, one will inevitably encounter it; for there is no escaping from sin.

It is said that when one looks back, there is no fixed place [of rebirth]; having not yet attained the tracks of the Path (mārga), one shall not meet with the end of life prematurely. This means that once the fifteen mental states have been attained, one cannot die prematurely;
one must necessarily attain these fifteen mental states before falling into the Path, and will subsequently progress upward to Arhatship.

Attaining the Way in the interim and not having one's life end in the interim constitutes three matters for the sake of ceasing the mind: namely, that while one’s wholesome or unwholesome intentions must necessarily attain the traces of the Way, they may also be destroyed midway;
likewise, death and rebirth cease, and wholesome intentions arise and then perish, yet the body does not die midway.
What is purity? That which consists of all objects of craving is impurity; the removal of craving is purity.
What are the characteristics of the five aggregates?
For example, fire is the aggregate (skandha) and the fuel is its characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
From the stage of "calming" (śamatha) up to "purity" (viśuddhi), these all constitute contemplation (vipaśyanā);
that is to say, one contemplates the characteristics of the body until, through śamatha and vipaśyanā, they return to purity, wherein their original nature is found to be non-existent.
Internally, one attends to counting the breaths; externally, one attends to severing the causes and conditions of evil—these are the two types of mental attention.
Question:
For what reason does one not first internally and externally contemplate the body, but instead first practice counting, following, stopping, contemplating, returning, and purifying?
As for the response:
because one’s mental application is impure, one does not see; once the body and mind are purified, one then fully perceives the internal and external paths of the body.
There are nineteen modes of practice, because humans have nineteen ailments, and thus there are also nineteen medicines.
Contemplating the body as foul is the medicine for ceasing lust;
mindfulness of the four immeasurable minds is the medicine for ceasing anger;
reflecting on what original causes and conditions led to one's own existence is the medicine for ceasing ignorance.
Anapanasmrti (mindfulness of breathing) is the medicine for excessive discursive thought.
One observes the body internally and externally.
What is meant by "body"?
What constitutes its substance?
The bones and flesh form the body, and the union of the six sense organs constitutes the substance.
What are these six sense organs?

That is to say: the eye meets with forms; the ear receives sounds; the nose turns toward fragrances; the mouth desires flavors; the body takes subtle touch as its object; the mind decays as its seed; and delusion serves as the root—thus there is the production of sentient beings.
Why is it that the body, both internal and external, is mentioned repeatedly?
It is because human craving and seeking involve degrees of magnitude and temporal sequence.
One must practice analytical contemplation regarding what one desires to obtain; such contemplation results in mindfulness, and mindfulness, arising from perception, constitutes knowledge.

Regarding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*): while sitting, one maintains the thought of arising; as one arises, the mind does not depart from that thought. Whatever the mind attends to and clings to during its activity constitutes consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is the application of mindfulness to the body.
When mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation ceases, what is meant by "the time when mindfulness ceases"?
It refers to the moment when the mindfulness of the breath’s exhaustion occurs, and the mental activity and the breath both cease.
When mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation ceases, it is like drawing in the sky; there is no place for birth and death, and the same applies to the path of the mind and mental states.
When the mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation ceases, one does not speak of the breath itself; rather, it is said that the mind and the breath cease.
When the mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation ceases, things arise from causes and conditions; the severance of their root constitutes the moment of cessation.
Regarding "observing the internal and external sensations": to observe means to see from where sensations arise; thus, observing them is what is meant by "observation.

As for "internal and external sensations": external desirable things are called external pleasant sensations (*sukha*), while external undesirable things are called external painful sensations (*duḥkha*);
internally, that which is agreeable is called internal pleasant sensation, while that which is disagreeable is called internal painful sensation.
That which is internal is the internal dharma; that which consists of external causes and conditions is the external dharma.
Furthermore, it is said that the eye is internal and form is external;
the ear is internal and sound is external.
The nose is internal, and fragrance is external;
the mouth is internal, and flavor is external;
the mind is internal, and thought is external.
To see something beautiful and smooth and desire to possess it is "itching";
to see something coarse and foul and feel aversion toward it is "pain.
Both fall into transgression.

Regarding the contemplation of the cessation of pain and itchiness: if a person’s arm is in pain, they do not direct their mind toward the pain; instead, they reflect that all other parts of the body experience pain in the same way. Because the mind does not dwell upon the pain, this serves to bring an end to the pain.
One may contemplate it, or one may not contemplate it; in contemplating pain, there is no attachment.
If you cherish your own body, you should contemplate the bodies of others;
if your mind cherishes the bodies of others, you should likewise contemplate your own body—this is also for the sake of cessation (*śamatha*).
Why are internal and external sensations (*vedanā*) mentioned twice?

This means that when people perceive forms, their attachments vary in degree—some are thin while others are thick—and because their mental perspectives are not equal, there are many differences between those who practice much and those who practice little.
One should carefully distinguish the path of contemplation: one should contemplate internally for the presence of delusion, and one should contemplate externally to realize it for oneself.
Physical and mental sensations are each distinct: experiencing cold, heat, or the extreme pain of knives and staves constitutes physical pain;
obtaining fine food, riding in a carriage, wearing beautiful clothes, and whatever else the body finds pleasant constitutes physical pleasure.
As for "heartache," it means that one is personally anxious and further worries about others and all manner of affairs; this is heartache.
When the mind attains what it desires and experiences various forms of joy, this is "itching of the heart."
Regarding the contemplation of mental characteristics, there are two causes and conditions for severing evil thoughts within:
first, one must restrain and eliminate the five pleasures and the six decays.

The observer observes the body; the body itself does not know its own coarseness or subtlety, but becomes aware of it only through perception—this is what is meant by "the mind observing the characteristics of the mind.
In this observation of the mind's characteristics, the breath is also the mind, and the counting is also the mind;
when one observes the breath while counting, this constitutes the mind observing the characteristics of the mind.

Regarding the contemplation of cessation (*śamatha*): it is to restrain desire for sensual pleasure, not to be restrained by desire for malice, not to be provoked by desire for ignorance, and not to act out of desire for greed; to seek no evil matters and to turn away from them all—this is the contemplation of cessation.
It is also said that cessation consists in knowing the *Saptatriṃśat-dharmasūtra* and constantly maintaining mindfulness without departing from it.
Regarding "observing the completion of exhalation and inhalation": "completion" (*kṣaya*) refers to the exhaustion of faults; "concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to the cessation of mental activity.
"Observing concentration" means observing the cessation that returns to purity;
"exhaustion and cessation" means that one can say, "I have explained this, understood this, and fully mastered this"—this is called exhaustion and cessation.
Regarding the breaths that have arisen: if one performs meritorious acts such as giving and all other wholesome dharmas, once they have arisen they immediately cease;

do they then follow after the mental intention? Countless instances of practicing unwholesome deeds in past and present lives likewise do not follow the mind in this manner. Others are also like this;
having already realized this, one should sever what has been severed, practicing the contemplation of cessation through the internal and external mind.
Regarding "internal and external phenomena": internal phenomena refer to one's own body, while external phenomena refer to others;
there are phenomena of observing the precepts and phenomena of not observing the precepts—these constitute internal and external phenomena.

Internal dharmas refer to practicing wisdom without departing from the *Saptatriṃśat-dharmasūtra*; as for all other matters, the mind does not fall into them. Practicing the Way and attaining the Way—this is what constitutes internal dharmas.
External phenomena refer to falling into birth and death; they refer to the activities of birth and death, through which one obtains birth and death.
Not being liberated from anything, one should sever what has yet to be severed; this constitutes the contemplation and cessation of internal and external phenomena.
Regarding the contemplation of the Dharma through cessation: all people take their own bodies as "the body," yet when one examines them with discernment, they are not the self's body. Why is this?
Although there is the eye and there are forms, the eye is not the body, and form is also not the body.
Why is this? When a person has died, although they possess eyes, there is nothing to be seen; likewise, although forms exist, there is no one to whom they correspond.
The body is thus: even when consciousness alone remains, it is no longer the body.

Why is this? Consciousness has no form and has no place where it can dwell; the same applies to the reckoning of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. To attain such a reckoning is called the meditative stilling through the contemplation of dharmas, and it is also called the stilling through non-recollection of evil.
Why is it that the recollection of evil does not cease?
It is because of the activity of the mind.
From the *Mahānāṇapāna-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Great Guarding of the Mind through Ānāpāna), Volume One.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-dharmatrātānuprekṣā-śīlavrata-sūtra*, Scroll II, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han:
One is self-aware of the exhalation and inhalation; one knows the exhalation and inhalation for oneself. At that time, it constitutes awareness. By means of this—
"Later comes 'knowing' (*jñāna*):

'awakening' (*bodha*) refers to awakening to the length and shortness of the breath; 'knowing' refers to knowing the arising and ceasing, the coarseness and subtlety, and the slowness and speed of the breath.

'Awakening to the cessation when exhalation and inhalation are exhausted' means awakening to the fact that the exhalation and inhalation are exhausted when one intends to respond [to them]; it also involves calculating how all things and the body arise and then cease."
"Stopping" refers to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
As for "seeing and contemplating emptiness," it means that by practicing the Path, one attains contemplation and no longer perceives a body.
"Falling into emptiness and non-existence" means that the mind has nothing to which it is attached.
When the mind has an object of attachment as its cause, there is the existence of the six sense bases; by severing these, one attains sagacity.
"Sagacity" refers to the body, and "clarity" refers to the Path.
To know from where one emerges and where one ceases is like being mindful of a stone emerging and a stone entering: once the wood and stone have entered, they are then extinguished.
The five aggregates are likewise: one emerges from form and enters sensation; emerges from sensation and enters perception;
emerges from perception and enters birth-and-death; and emerges from birth-and-death and enters consciousness. Having made these distinctions, one then enters the *Saptatriṃśat-dharmasūtra*.
Question:
What is the contemplation of the unconditioned path? Answer:

"Thinking" (*cintā*) refers to deliberation; "contemplation" (*manana*) refers to listening. It does not mean being oblivious to the myriad things; rather, it means acting according to what has been taught. Since the Way is attained through such practice, it is said that through thinking and contemplation, one realizes the Way of non-action (*wuwei*).
"Reflection" (*cintā*) refers to mindfulness; "contemplation" (*vitarka*) refers to the discrimination between black and white.
"Black" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), while "white" refers to the Path (*mārga*).

Since the Path is non-existent, once one has discriminated that which is non-existent, there is nothing further to be done; therefore, it is said that contemplation is the unconditioned Path (*asaṃskṛta-mārga*).
If one calculates that there is something to be done or something to which to cling, this constitutes non-contemplation.
Thought itself is an object; contemplation is for the purpose of understanding the mind.
Once the mind is understood, one then knows the reality of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Furthermore, "si" (thought) is called "nian" (mindfulness), and "wei" (deliberation) is called "ji" (calculation).

To sever birth and death and attain the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) means that when the mind has something to which it is attached, it is "birth," and when it has nothing to which it is attached, it is "death."
One who has attained the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) is able to fly; therefore, it is said that birth and death (*saṃsāra*) must be severed.
There are five meanings for attaining the supernormal powers:
the first is joy (*prīti*).
Second is faith; third is diligence;
fourth is concentration;
Fifth is supernormal power (*abhijñā*).

By practicing the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) without exhausting one's strength, one attains the five supernormal powers; by exhausting one's strength with mastery, one moves toward the six supernormal powers. For a practitioner of the Way, the four bases of psychic power lead to the attainment of the five supernormal powers. If one exhausts one's intent, one may attain the six supernormal powers. "Exhausting one's intent" means that the mind has no further desire for worldly phenomena.
First, faith; second, diligence;
third, intentionality.
Fourth, concentration;
fifth, wisdom—these five things constitute the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
When mindfulness is added as a faculty, there are six things in total.
Faith is associated with the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): mindfulness, joy, diligence, concentration, and wisdom; these are what are associated with the five faculties (*indriya*).
From the concentration of joy, one speaks of the path of faith;
from the concentration of power, one speaks of diligence;
from the concentration of intention, one speaks of the concentration of mental attention.
From the concentration of giving, it is called the practice of the Path.
Because there are roots for the sake of seeds, all conditioned phenomena are considered evil; thus, perceptions arise, and one cannot attain victory.
This means that attaining dhyāna is due to the power [of concentration]; it is also said that evil cannot overcome wholesome intention.
Because [the mind] ceases and then arises again, it is called "power.
One whose concentration is powerful cannot be destroyed when evil intentions arise.
Because of wholesome intention, it constitutes the concentration of power (*balasamādhi*).
When a practitioner on the path has not yet attained contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), they should apply analytical investigation to attain it.
When the mind remains fixed upon the object of observation and no longer wavers, this constitutes the attainment of contemplation.
The first method for ceasing evil is the practice of seated meditation (*dhyāna*).

The second method is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which at times involves contemplating the body, at times contemplating the mind, at times contemplating the breath, and at times contemplating existence or non-existence; one should practice these various contemplations according to the specific conditions and causes present.
Cessation is one dharma; contemplation is two dharmas. When evil is exhausted, cessation and contemplation constitute the path of contemplation.
As long as evil is not yet exhausted, one does not see the Path; only when evil is exhausted does one attain the path of contemplation.

The single method for ceasing evil is the knowledge of evil. To restrain all things and not allow the mind to cling is called cessation; it is also the attainment of the cessation that follows the perception of tranquility.
The attainment of the cessation that follows the perception of tranquility is the single method for ceasing evil.
When evil has ceased, one attains insight (*vipaśyanā*).
For the sake of observing these two dharmas, for the sake of attaining the Four Noble Truths, and for the sake of practicing purity, one should further cultivate purity:
by recognizing suffering and abandoning its origin, and by knowing cessation and practicing the path. This is like the clarity at sunrise, for it turns toward and emerges through the twelve gates.
The Sūtra says:
"One attains liberation through the Path.
One leaves behind darkness and beholds light, just as when the sun rises; for example, when the sun rises, much is seen, because all darkness has been discarded.
The obscure is suffering; how is it known to be suffering?
Because there are many obstructions, it is known to be suffering.
What is the abandoning of habitual tendencies?
It refers to non-action.
What is the realization of exhaustion?
It refers to non-existence.
The Way consists of clearly understanding suffering, severing its origins, realizing its cessation, and contemplating the path.
Awareness arises from suffering; when one does not grasp at suffering, there is no longer any awareness—this is the nature of suffering.
"Realizing exhaustion" means knowing that human life is exhausted.
"Realizing that one must undergo old age, sickness, and death" means knowing that all things are destined to perish; this is what is meant by realizing exhaustion.
It is like the rising sun performing four tasks:
First, the destruction of darkness, meaning that wisdom is able to destroy delusion;
second, the vision of light, meaning that once delusion is removed, wisdom alone remains;
third, the vision of the myriad forms of things, meaning that one perceives all the impurities belonging to the body.
Fourth, regarding the maturation of all things: were there no sun or moon, all things would not ripen;
likewise, if a person lacks wisdom and is mired in delusion, their mind will not ripen either.

As for those who practice both the higher [wisdom] and the concurrent [conduct], they have already performed the deeds to be done and do not engage in discursive discrimination; this refers to practicing the five right paths of speech, wherein body and mind are practiced in unison.
From the true recollection of dharmas, the mind becomes attached within those dharmas;

from the true recollection of dharmas, the mind becomes attached to that which is recollected, whereby it gives rise to this very state: seeking birth-and-death, one obtains birth-and-death; seeking the Way, one obtains the Way.
To follow the mind as it arises internally and externally is what constitutes mindfulness of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*).

When the mind is fixed upon the Dharma, one knows for oneself from within the Four Noble Truths: "This is to be attained," "this is not to arise," "this is not to be acquired," and "this is to be abandoned. Thus, the mind becomes fearful and does not dare to transgress.
That whatever one practices and whatever one contemplates is always centered on the Path—this is what is meant by "the mind being attached to the Dharma.
This is called the Dharma; it correctly arises from the root of the Truths, yet its root is attachment to the mind.
"Dharma" refers to the Way and its teachings.
"Following the Truths" refers to the Four Noble Truths.
"That which fundamentally arises from the mind" means that all matters within the cycle of birth and death toward which one is directed fundamentally arise from the mind.
When the mind becomes attached, the five aggregates arise.
The mind should be severed; when the root is severed, the five aggregates are severed.

At times, one severs them spontaneously without conscious thought, yet the mind may still give rise to offenses on its own, or remain unsettled in the Path and commit offenses, because [the afflictions] have not yet been exhausted.

When the mind is attached to dharmas, it contemplates all things with focused attention; this constitutes falling into external dharmas. When the mind does not contemplate all things, it constitutes falling into the dharmas of the Path.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute the phenomena of birth and death, while the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) constitute the phenomena of the Path.

To have the mind "attached to the phenomena" means to restrain the five aggregates so as not to transgress them, and also to constantly keep the Path in mind without departing from it; this is what is meant by having the mind attached to the phenomena.
That which is fundamentally correct: externally, it serves as the foundation for all things and the locus of merit;
internally, it is collectively comprised of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, for the practice of the Way does not occur in a single moment or at a single point.

That which is called the "basis" refers to practicing the Dharma of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment according to their proper sequence; because the mind does not enter into error and remains correct, it is termed the "correct basis."

That which is fundamental is the correct; each follows its own distinct practice. One takes non-action (*wuwei*) as the counterpart to the fundamental, and non-seeking as the counterpart to the correct.

One takes non-action as the counterpart to non-action, and non-permanence as the counterpart to the Way (*dao*). Taking non-existence as the counterpart to that which has no place, no fundamental, and no correctness, it constitutes "nothingness."
One experiences the body through the awakening of concentration; such is the path of the Dharma, which is called the "Dharma of concentration.
As for the "proclaimer of the path," this refers to one who explains the causes and conditions from which the path is attained.
To "perceive the aggregates" means to experience the five aggregates.
There is "entering," which means entering into the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Because there are the aggregates of birth and death, one receives what is correct;
as for "correctness," the Way is inherently correct, and one need only rectify one's own mind.

When a person practices *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), they attain counting, attainment of the signs, following, and cessation; thus they experience joy. These are the four kinds [of joy].
It is like drilling for fire: seeing smoke cannot cook anything—what kind of joy would that be?
This is because one has not yet attained the essential way out.
In the practice of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), there are eighteen afflictions that prevent a person from following the Path:

first, sensual desire; second, ill-will; third, delusion; fourth, frivolous pleasure; fifth, pride; sixth, doubt; seventh, failure to attend to the characteristics of practice; eighth, attending to the characteristics of others; ninth, lack of mindfulness; tenth, distracted thoughts; eleventh, incomplete mindfulness; twelfth, excessive exertion; thirteenth, insufficient exertion; fourteenth, fear and trepidation; fifteenth, forced restraint of the mind; sixteenth, anxiety; seventeenth, haste; eighteenth, failing to transcend mental activity through attachment—these are the eighteen afflictions.
Not guarding these eighteen causes and conditions prevents one from attaining the Way; by guarding them, one attains the Way.

Regarding "not undertaking the practice of characteristics," this means not contemplating the thirty-two things and not recollecting the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; this is what is meant by not undertaking the practice of characteristics.

"Grasping at the characteristics of another" means that before one has attained the ten breaths, one immediately practices following the characteristics; this is grasping at the characteristics of another.
"Another's mindfulness" means that when inhaling, one is mindful of exhaling, and when exhaling, one is mindful of inhaling; this is another's mindfulness.
"Incomplete mindfulness" refers to when one has not yet attained the first dhyāna but already thinks of the second dhyāna; this is called incomplete mindfulness.

"Forcibly restraining the mind" refers to when the mind is distracted while sitting and cannot find rest; one should then practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) or recite the sūtras so that the distraction does not arise—this is called forcibly restraining the mind.
Vigorous effort constitutes wisdom; it proceeds through these six matters, namely: counting the breaths, following, stopping, contemplating, returning, and purifying—these are the six.
What is panting? What is breathing?
What is the vital breath?
What are the powers? What are the winds? That which is panting is the wind of the mind’s respiration;

it is the guardian of life, the vital breath, and the wind of sight and hearing. It is that which enables speech, the strength for bending and stretching according to the Way, and the ability to lift heavy objects and manifest anger.
One must attain the Way through the guarding of the mind (manasikāra). By what means is the guarding of the mind attained?
It is attained through counting and shifting; from shifting comes the attainment of following the breath, and the same applies to cessation, contemplation, and returning to purity.
When practicing the Way and desiring to bring the mind to rest, one should understand three matters:

First, one must first contemplate the body and consider from where it originally comes; it exists only through the activity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and by severing these five aggregates, it will no longer arise.
It is like a temporary lodging for a mere moment. If the mind does not yet understand this, one should contemplate the ninefold path (*navāṅga-dharma*) to realize it for oneself.
Second, one should internally observe within the mind as the breath enters and exits.
Third, at the moment when the mindfulness of the exhalation and inhalation ceases:
when the breath has been exhaled and is slightly light, and the mindfulness ceases, what is it that knows there is nothing?
When the mind is concentrated, one knows emptiness; knowing emptiness, one knows non-existence. Why is this?

Because if the breath ceases and is not renewed, one dies; thus one knows that the body is merely produced by the vital energy (*prāṇa*). When the energy is extinguished, it becomes empty; realizing this emptiness is to enter the Path.
Therefore, there are three matters for practicing the Way:
first, contemplating the body;
second, maintaining single-minded mindfulness.
Third, mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
first, the cessation of bodily pain and itching;
Second, ceasing vocal sounds;
third, ceasing mental activities—these six matters lead to the swift attainment of tranquility.
The Essential Sūtra says:
A single thought refers to one mind; a proximate thought refers to calculating the body; many thoughts refer to one mind; and non-separation from thought refers to not being separated from thought.
When one practices these four matters through bodily conduct, one will swiftly attain tranquility.
